stage1Body.text: The line is split on shell operators (; && || | &). Each segment is evaluated independently and the first denied segment refuses the whole line, so a blocked stage cannot ride on an allowed one.

stage2Body.text: Before tokenizing, the raw segment is scanned for command substitution $(...) and backticks, parameter expansion ${...}, process substitution <(...), and ANSI-C / hex / unicode escapes ($'...'). Any hit is denied immediately â the engine will not try to

stage3Body.text: The segment is tokenized into an argument vector using shell-like quoting rules. An unparsable segment (unbalanced quotes, etc.) is treated as obfuscated and denied.

stage4Body.text: Leading wrappers are peeled off so policy sees the real inner program: sudo (and its -u/-g options), env (and its options + VAR=val assignments), the flagless wrappers nohup, nice, command, exec, time, setsid, stdbuf, ionice, timeout and a leading backslash, and shells (bash, sh, dash, zsh, ash, ksh, csh, tcsh) â a shell with -c has its inner command string re-tokenized (e.g. bash -c

stage5Body.text: After stripping, the argv is checked for eval of dynamic input and base64-decode pipelines. These are denied because they hide the eventual command from static inspection.

stage6Body.text: Every token is lowercased and the argv is joined by single spaces to form the canonical command; a whitespace-collapsed form is also produced to defeat keyword-splitting tricks. Matching always runs against these canonical forms, never the raw string.

stage7Body.text: The always-on baseline dangerous-command blocklist is applied first and can never be re-enabled by an operator allow rule (deny-wins). Then operator deny rules (deny always wins), then â if a fail-closed allowlist is enforced â anything not matched by an allow rule is denied.
